questions.stem: A 31 year old man dislocates his shoulder playing football. As the doctor examines it in the Emergency Department he says he feels sick and sweaty, goes pale and slumps in the chair. He is unresponsive for about 20 seconds and then is fully alert and orientated. He has no past medical history. His ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pain is a classic trigger for vasovagal (reflex) syncope: a prodrome of nausea and sweating, brief LOC and rapid full recovery.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Painful trigger + prodrome + brief LOC + **rapid full recovery**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reflex faint triggered by pain: **vasovagal syncope**.

elim: He is alert immediately with no post-ictal confusion.
Does not resolve in seconds without treatment.
Follows standing up, not pain while seated.
He has no cardiac history, a normal ECG and a clear painful trigger.

steps.x: **D. Vasovagal syncope.** Triggers: prolonged standing, heat, emotion, pain, medical procedures.

questions.stem: A 14 year old girl has her HPV vaccination at school. A minute later she says her ears are ringing and her vision is blurred. She slides off the chair and is unresponsive for 15 seconds. She then wakes and knows where she is. She has no rash, wheeze or swelling. Her pulse rate is 56 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Medical procedures such as injections trigger vasovagal syncope; a slow pulse and low BP with no rash or wheeze separate it from anaphylaxis.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Needle trigger, prodrome, slow pulse, no allergic features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Vasovagal syncope**, not anaphylaxis.

elim: Absences have no prodrome and no collapse.
Gives rash, wheeze, swelling and a fast pulse, and does not recover in seconds.
Does not recover in seconds on its own.
A rare arrhythmic cause; the needle trigger and prodrome point to a reflex faint.

steps.x: **D. Vasovagal syncope.** After an injection: slow pulse + no rash = faint; fast pulse + rash + wheeze = anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man collapses while standing at a long graduation ceremony on a warm day. A witness says he went grey, fell, and both arms jerked for about 5 seconds. He did not bite his tongue. Within a minute he was talking normally and knew where he was. His examination and ECG are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A faint after prolonged standing in heat can include a few seconds of jerking; the key difference from a seizure is no post-ictal phase.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: standing at a long graduation ceremony
Within a minute he was talking normally
steps.x: Standing + heat + pallor + brief jerks + **no post-ictal phase**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Convulsive faint: **vasovagal syncope**.

elim: Has no prodrome and often follows exertion; his ECG is normal.
Would leave a post-ictal phase of confusion and drowsiness.
Does not recover within a minute on its own.
Usually prolonged, with eyes closed and no pallor.

steps.x: **E. Vasovagal syncope.** Brief jerks can occur in a faint; post-ictal confusion means seizure.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman faints after standing up from a long, very hot bath. She felt warm and lightheaded and her vision went dark first. Her partner found her on the floor and she came round within 30 seconds, fully alert. She has no chest pain or palpitations and takes no medication. Her ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Heat is a classic trigger: vasodilation and pooling set off the reflex, giving a simple faint with prodrome and rapid recovery.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Heat trigger + prodrome + quick full recovery + normal ECG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A simple faint: **vasovagal syncope**.

elim: Causes exertional syncope with a murmur in older patients.
Has no warm, dark-vision prodrome and leaves confusion.
Causes exertional syncope; her ECG is normal.
Rarely causes loss of consciousness and gives focal deficits.

steps.x: **E. Vasovagal syncope.** Heat + standing + prodrome + rapid recovery = vasovagal.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man is queuing for 2 hours outside a stadium on a summer afternoon. He briefly loses consciousness and recovers fully within a minute. He has no injuries and no history of heart disease. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg after the event. His friend says he looked pale and clammy just before.
questions.q: Which symptom is he most likely to describe just before he fell?
o: Sweating, nausea and ringing in the ears
Unpleasant smell and a rising feeling in the stomach
questions.e: Vasovagal syncope has a prodrome: feeling warm, sweating, nausea, lightheadedness, blurred or tunnel vision and ringing in the ears.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Prolonged standing, pale and clammy, quick recovery = **vasovagal**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The vasovagal prodrome: **sweating, nausea and ringing in the ears**.

elim: Suggests cardiac ischaemia, a red flag.
Suggests an arrhythmic cause, a red flag.
No warning suggests a cardiac cause.
A temporal lobe aura of a focal seizure.

steps.x: **D. Sweating, nausea and ringing in the ears.** Prodrome = warm, sweaty, nauseated, lightheaded, blurred vision, tinnitus.

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman faints at a friend's wedding after standing through a long service. She had felt hot and sick and her vision narrowed before she fell. Her friends ask how long she is likely to be unconscious and how she will feel afterwards. She has no medical history.
questions.q: Which is the most likely course of her episode?
o: Brief loss of consciousness with rapid, full recovery
Recovery with a persisting one-sided weakness
Recovery with confusion lasting an hour
Recovery with severe headache and vomiting
questions.e: In vasovagal syncope, loss of consciousness is brief (seconds to minutes) with a rapid full recovery and no confusion afterwards.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Standing + prodrome = classic vasovagal faint.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Brief loss of consciousness with rapid, full recovery.**

elim: Far too long for a faint; suggests another cause.
A focal deficit suggests stroke.
A post-ictal picture, suggesting seizure.
Suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: **A. Brief loss of consciousness with rapid, full recovery.** Vasovagal: seconds to minutes of LOC, back to normal quickly.

questions.stem: A 34 year old scaffolder has had several vasovagal faints, each after standing for a long time in the heat with a typical prodrome and rapid recovery. His examination and ECG are normal. He asks what the main danger of his condition is.
questions.q: Which is the main risk of his condition?
questions.e: Vasovagal syncope is benign; the main risk is injury from falling during the faint, which matters more for someone who works at height.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Benign faints, but he works **at height**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The danger is the fall: **injury from a fall**.

elim: Faints do not lead to epilepsy.
Vasovagal syncope is benign and does not damage the heart.
Faints do not cause stroke.
A risk of arrhythmic syncope, not vasovagal syncope.

steps.x: **C. Injury from a fall.** Vasovagal syncope's main complication is injury from a fall.

questions.stem: A 23 year old man is attached to a cardiac monitor before a minor procedure. As the cannula goes in he feels sick and hot and loses consciousness for 10 seconds. The nurse records his observations during the episode. He recovers fully within a minute. Before the cannula his pulse was 78 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely set of observations during the episode?
o: Pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 70/40 mmHg
Pulse rate 150 bpm and BP 150/90 mmHg
Pulse rate 180 bpm and BP 80/50 mmHg
Pulse rate 40 bpm and BP 74/40 mmHg
Pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg
questions.e: Vasovagal syncope is a reflex syncope with a transient drop in both heart rate and blood pressure.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Needle trigger, prodrome, rapid recovery = **vasovagal**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Both fall: **pulse 40 bpm and BP 74/40 mmHg**.

elim: Tachycardia with hypotension suggests hypovolaemia or anaphylaxis.
Suggests a tachyarrhythmia or a stress response.
Suggests a tachyarrhythmia such as SVT or VT.
No change would not explain loss of consciousness.

steps.x: **D. Pulse rate 40 bpm and BP 74/40 mmHg.** Vasovagal = transient bradycardia + hypotension.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man is a guest at a long outdoor wedding and has stood for 90 minutes in the sun. He feels dizzy and nauseated, then collapses. He comes round within 30 seconds, fully alert. He has no chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness. His pulse rate is 68 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg and his ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Vasovagal syncope presents as a simple faint, classically after prolonged standing, with a prodrome and rapid full recovery.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: stood for 90 minutes in the sun
steps.x: Prolonged standing + heat + prodrome + rapid recovery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Simple faint** (vasovagal syncope).

elim: Gives syncope without a prodrome and a slow pulse with an abnormal ECG.
Gives breathlessness, tachycardia and chest pain.
Gives a thunderclap headache and may not recover quickly.
Gives vertigo and focal signs on neck movement.

steps.x: **C. Simple faint.** Simple faint = vasovagal syncope.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman hears on the phone that her father has died. She feels lightheaded, hot and sick, then collapses at her desk. A colleague says she was pale and floppy for about 15 seconds and then came round, upset but fully orientated. She has no chest pain. Her pulse rate is 64 bpm and her ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Emotional stress is a classic vasovagal trigger: an exaggerated vagal reflex with a prodrome, brief LOC and full recovery.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Emotional shock + prodrome + brief LOC + full recovery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Emotion-triggered reflex faint: **vasovagal syncope**.

elim: Gives tingling and carpopedal spasm, rarely loss of consciousness.
Causes chest pain and ECG changes after emotional stress.
Causes memory loss without collapse.
Gives vertigo and focal brainstem signs, not a vagal prodrome after bad news.

steps.x: **D. Vasovagal syncope.** Emotional stress is a classic trigger for vasovagal syncope.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy collapses in a hot school assembly. A teacher saw him go pale and slump, with a few jerks of his arms. He regained consciousness after 20 seconds. His mother is worried he has epilepsy. His examination is normal.
questions.q: Which feature of the episode most strongly supports a faint rather than a seizure?
questions.e: Brief jerks can happen in a faint; the absence of a post-ictal phase (no confusion or drowsiness afterwards) is the key feature separating vasovagal syncope from a seizure.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: a few jerks of his arms
steps.x: Heat, pallor, short LOC with brief jerks: likely a faint. What separates faint from fit?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **No confusion afterwards** (no post-ictal phase).

elim: Occurs in both.
Can occur in both, so it does not separate them.
Can occur in both faints and seizures.
Occurs in both.

steps.x: **E. No confusion afterwards.** Faint vs fit: no post-ictal phase = faint.

questions.stem: A 20 year old student has fainted twice in 6 months, both times while standing in hot crowded rooms, with a typical prodrome of warmth, nausea and dimming vision and full recovery within a minute. Her examination, lying and standing BP and 12-lead ECG are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
o: A clinical diagnosis from the history
questions.e: Vasovagal syncope is a clinical diagnosis based on the classic history (trigger, prodrome, rapid recovery) once the ECG is normal.

steps.x: **A. A clinical diagnosis from the history.** Vasovagal syncope is diagnosed clinically; the ECG excludes cardiac causes.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man fainted at a bus stop after standing for 30 minutes on a hot day. He felt sweaty and lightheaded beforehand and recovered fully within a minute. He is now well. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG is recorded in the Emergency Department.
questions.q: Which is the main purpose of the ECG?
o: To exclude a cardiac arrhythmic cause
To measure the length of the faint
questions.e: A 12-lead ECG is the first-line test in all transient loss of consciousness, to exclude cardiac arrhythmic causes such as long QT, Brugada, WPW or heart block.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.

steps.x: **C. To exclude a cardiac arrhythmic cause.** Every blackout gets a 12-lead ECG to exclude arrhythmia (NICE CG109).

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman faints in a queue at the post office on a warm day. She felt hot and nauseated first and recovered within a minute. She has very heavy periods. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her 12-lead ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation?
questions.e: Basic bloods form part of the general syncope work-up; with heavy periods, a full blood count looks for anaemia that can lower the threshold for fainting.

Typical faint with a normal ECG, plus heavy periods.

No neurological features.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman is on a cardiac monitor in the Emergency Department while a nurse takes blood. She says she feels hot and sick, goes pale and briefly loses consciousness, then recovers fully within 30 seconds. The rhythm strip at the moment she lost consciousness is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Rhythm strip at loss of consciousness
visual.caption: Sinus rhythm at 36 bpm: vagal sinus bradycardia.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the rhythm strip?
questions.e: The vagal reflex causes a sudden parasympathetic sinus bradycardia, with vasodilation from sympathetic withdrawal; the rhythm stays sinus.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Needle trigger and prodrome = vasovagal; the vagus slows the sinus node.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Every P wave followed by a QRS, but slow: **sinus bradycardia**.

elim: Irregularly irregular; not a reflex response.
Shows P waves unrelated to QRS complexes; would not recover in seconds after a needle.
A fast narrow-complex rhythm.
A fast broad-complex rhythm.

steps.x: **C. Sinus bradycardia.** Vasovagal: vagal sinus bradycardia plus vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 15 year old girl fainted at a concert after standing for 3 hours. She had felt hot and sick and recovered within a minute. Her examination, lying and standing BP and ECG are normal. Her mother is worried and asks for a brain scan and a referral to a heart specialist.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure and explain it is a benign condition
Referral to a first seizure clinic
questions.e: Uncomplicated vasovagal syncope with a normal ECG is benign; the first-line management is reassurance and explanation.

Typical faint, normal ECG, worried parent.

Not needed with a typical history and normal ECG.
Nothing suggests seizure.
Drugs are not needed for uncomplicated vasovagal syncope.

steps.x: **B. Reassure and explain it is a benign condition.** Vasovagal syncope: reassure; no scans or referrals with a typical history.

questions.stem: A 29 year old nurse has had three vasovagal faints in a year, each during long shifts standing in a hot operating theatre. Each time she had a prodrome and recovered quickly. Her ECG and examination are normal. She asks how to prevent further episodes.

The opposite of what helps; hydration helps.

Not recommended for vasovagal syncope.

steps.x: **C. Stay well hydrated and avoid standing still for long periods.** Vasovagal advice: avoid prolonged standing and heat, stay hydrated.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man is sitting upright in a dentist's chair before a tooth extraction. He suddenly says he feels very hot, sick and that his vision is going grey. He is pale and sweaty but still conscious. His pulse rate is 48 bpm.

o: Give a glass of water and keep him sitting upright
Lie him flat and raise his legs
Stand him up and walk him outside
questions.e: If a vasovagal prodrome occurs, lying down and elevating the legs restores cerebral perfusion and can prevent loss of consciousness.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Prodrome now, still conscious: act before he faints.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lie him flat and raise his legs.**

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has had four typical vasovagal faints over 2 years, each with a clear trigger and prodrome and quick full recovery. He has had no injuries. His ECG and examination are normal. He read online about tablets for fainting and asks whether he should take one.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Uncomplicated vasovagal syncope typically needs no pharmacological treatment; reassurance and trigger avoidance are enough.

steps.x: **C. No medication with trigger advice.** Vasovagal syncope: no drugs for uncomplicated cases.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman has fainted in a hot shop queue. She is lying on the floor, breathing normally, pale and sweaty, and has been unconscious for about 10 seconds. Her radial pulse is slow and weak. A bystander wants to sit her up and give her a drink.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Give her a drink of water
Keep her lying flat and raise her legs
Sit her upright against a wall
questions.e: Keeping her flat with her legs raised increases venous return, restores cerebral perfusion and ends the episode.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
A faint in progress, breathing with a pulse.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Keep her lying flat and raise her legs.**

steps.x: **B. Keep her lying flat and raise her legs.** Faint: flat, legs up; never sit or stand them up.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man faints while watching his own blood being taken. His pulse rate fell from 88 to 38 bpm in a few seconds and then recovered. A medical student asks which nerve slowed his heart so quickly.
questions.q: Which nerve is most likely responsible for his bradycardia?
questions.e: Vasovagal syncope is a sudden parasympathetic (vagal) outflow that slows the sinus node, with sympathetic withdrawal causing vasodilation.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.

clues: watching his own blood being taken
from 88 to 38 bpm in a few seconds
steps.x: Sudden reflex slowing = **parasympathetic** outflow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The heart's parasympathetic supply: **vagus nerve**.

elim: Carries afferent signals from the carotid sinus, not efferent slowing of the heart.
Supplies the diaphragm.
Supplies the larynx.
Speed the heart up.

steps.x: **E. Vagus nerve.** Vasovagal: vagal bradycardia plus sympathetic withdrawal vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with recurrent vasovagal syncope has a tilt table test. When he faints, his heart rate falls to 40 bpm and BP to 70/40 mmHg. In a repeat test after IV atropine his heart rate stays at 80 bpm, but his BP still falls to 78/44 mmHg and he feels faint.

o: Excess vagal slowing of the heart
questions.e: The vasovagal reflex has two parts: vagal bradycardia (blocked by atropine) and vasodilation from sympathetic withdrawal; the fall in systemic vascular resistance still drops BP.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.
Atropine removed the vagal slowing, but BP still fell.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The other limb: **vasodilation from sympathetic withdrawal**.

elim: Atropine has blocked this; his heart rate stays at 80 bpm.

There is no allergic reaction.

steps.x: **A. Arteriolar vasodilation from sympathetic withdrawal.** Vasovagal = cardioinhibitory (vagal) + vasodepressor (sympathetic withdrawal).

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman faints after standing in a hot queue. Her BP drops to 68/40 mmHg and pulse rate to 42 bpm for about 20 seconds, during which she is unconscious. She recovers fully once lying down. A student asks why a low BP for only 20 seconds causes unconsciousness.

o: Cerebral perfusion falling below the level needed for consciousness
Electrical seizure discharge in the cortex
questions.e: The fall in cardiac output and vascular resistance drops BP, reducing cerebral perfusion below the threshold needed to keep consciousness; restoring it brings rapid recovery.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.
Brief fall in BP, brief LOC, fixed by lying flat.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

questions.stem: A 23 year old man feels faint while donating blood. His BP falls to 80/46 mmHg. The nurse lies him flat and raises his legs, and within a minute his BP rises to 112/70 mmHg and he feels well. The trend is shown (see item resources).

questions.e: Raising the legs uses gravity to increase venous return (preload), raising cardiac output and restoring cerebral perfusion, which ends the episode.

steps.x: Recovery within a minute of a posture change = **gravity**.

Not the main effect of a postural change.

steps.x: **B. Increased venous return raising cardiac output.** Legs up = more venous return = more cardiac output = brain perfused.

questions.stem: A 16 year old girl faints in a hot classroom. A video taken by a friend shows her slump and have several irregular jerks of her arms and legs for 4 seconds. She is alert and chatting within a minute. An EEG later is normal. Her parents ask why she jerked if this was not a seizure.

steps.x: **E. Transient cerebral hypoperfusion.** Jerks in a faint = hypoperfusion, not epilepsy.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man stands still for 40 minutes at a hot outdoor memorial service. Blood pools in his legs. He feels warm and sick, then faints for 15 seconds and recovers fully. His ECG and examination are normal. A student asks what starts the faint in the first place.

o: An arrhythmia from a structural heart problem
